result.question: If hydrogen starts climbing on Transformer 1 at site MAIN, I want my operators to know what to suspect and what to check next. Using our known transformer failure modes, list every mode where rising hydrogen is a meaningful signal. For each one, say which one or two companion channels would confirm it, choosing from methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co, co2, oxygen, dbds, dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v and oti. Then look at the actual data between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 and tell me which of those modes the companion channels currently support. Run a DGA fault classification on the latest complete sample as a tie-breaker. Keep the list to the modes where hydrogen genuinely helps tell them apart, not every mode. If hydrogen didn't rise across the window, say so, but still give the watch-list, and label every mode as 'not currently indicated' rather than ranking them.
result.answer:
## Hydrogen watch-list for Transformer 1 (site MAIN)

**Data check (2024-01-15 → 2024-01-19): hydrogen did NOT rise across the window.** It oscillated between 2,800 and 2,950 ppm (mean ~2,874, no upward trend — the 16th's 2,950 spike reversed by the 17th). Note that the absolute level is very high, but the requested rising trend is absent. Per your instruction, the full watch-list follows, all labeled **not currently indicated**.

### Modes where rising hydrogen is a genuinely discriminating signal

| Failure mode | Confirm with (companion channels) | Status vs. current data |
|---|---|---|
| **Partial Discharge in Oil** | methane (H2+CH4 dominant, low heavier gases), co2 | **Not currently indicated** — methane (~7,350) is elevated but stable, not trending with H2 |
| **Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating** | ethylene, methane (T1/T2 signature) | **Not currently indicated** — ethylene is very high (~16,600) but flat across the window |
| **Thermal Fault — Core/Winding** | ethylene, ethane | **Not currently indicated** — both elevated but stable; no H2 co-trend |
| **Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking)** | acetylene, methane | **Not currently indicated** — acetylene is essentially absent (6–8 ppm) |
| **High-Energy Arcing** | acetylene, ethylene | **Not currently indicated** — acetylene ~7 ppm flat; would need C2H2 climbing alongside C2H4 |

*Excluded per your "genuinely helps tell them apart" rule:* Oil Contamination/Moisture Ingress, Oil Dielectric Degradation (diagnosed by dbds, dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v — hydrogen adds little); Cellulose Insulation Ageing (CO/CO2-driven; CO is very low here at 30–35 ppm, so not indicated either); Tap Changer Mechanical Wear (mechanical/absent C2H2, H2 not discriminating).

### DGA tie-breaker — Rogers Ratio (IEC 60599)

The DGA interpretation tool was unavailable (LLM error), so the ratios were computed directly from the latest complete sample (2024-01-18): H2 = 2,900, CH4 = 7,350, C2H6 = 5,450, C2H4 = 16,600, C2H2 = 7 ppm.

- r1 = CH4/H2 = 2.53 → code **2**
- r2 = C2H2/C2H4 = 0.0004 → code **0**
- r3 = C2H4/C2H6 = 3.04 → code **2**

**Rogers code 0-2-2 → thermal fault in the 300–700 °C range (medium-temperature thermal fault)** — consistent with heavy hydrocarbon generation (ethylene-dominant) rather than PD or arcing. Even this classification reflects an existing, static thermal condition; nothing in the window shows an active hydrogen-driven escalation.

### Bottom line for operators
No rising hydrogen in this window, so no mode is currently indicated. Keep the five-mode watch-list active; the first thing to check on any confirmed H2 climb is **acetylene** (rules arcing in/out) and **ethylene** (thermal), with **methane** as the PD pointer. The standing Rogers result (thermal fault 300–700 °C with an already-elevated H2 baseline of ~2,900 ppm) warrants a re-sample and oil-condition check (dbds, dielectric rigidity) regardless of the flat trend.
